section_1.title: Prerequisite & Intuition: The 'Language' of Coordinates
section_1.content: Define a basis as a coordinate system (a set of grid lines). Visualize the standard basis (x, y) as a square grid. Explain that a point (3, 2) is just a set of instructions: '3 steps along the red vector, 2 steps along the blue vector'.
section_1.example: Imagine a character 'Pixel' living on a standard grid. The basis vectors {i, j} are his compass directions North and East.

section_2.title: The Problem: Changing Perspectives
section_2.content: Introduce a new 'tilted' basis. Show how the same point in space now needs different numbers to be described. Emphasize that the point hasn't moved, but our perspective has shifted.
section_2.example: Pixel wears 'Magic Goggles' that tilt his world by 45 degrees. To him, the same stationary tree now looks like it's at different coordinate values.

section_3.title: The Mechanism: The Transition Matrix (P)
section_3.content: Formally derive the transition matrix P, where columns are the new basis vectors expressed in terms of the old basis. Equation: [v]_old = P * [v]_new. Use animation to show the mapping process.
section_3.example: If the new basis vectors are {1,1} and {-1,1}, demonstrate how to build matrix P = [[1, -1], [1, 1]] to transform old coordinates to new ones.

section_4.title: Application: Why Do We Care?
section_4.content: Explain that we choose bases to make calculations easier (e.g., diagonalization). Use a visual of a complex shape that looks complicated in standard basis but becomes a simple rectangle in a 'smarter' basis.
section_4.example: A robot arm (the device) calculating joint angles. It’s easier to describe the 'hand' position relative to the 'shoulder' (local basis) rather than the 'room' origin (global basis).

section_5.title: Summary & Reflection
section_5.content: Recap: (1) Basis = coordinate system, (2) Transition Matrix = translator between systems. Remind students: The space is invariant; only the description changes.
section_5.example: Final shot: A map of a park. The map stays the same, but you can describe a treasure’s location starting from the 'Front Gate' or the 'Old Oak Tree'. Both are correct; one might just be easier for the treasure hunter.
